name: AWS DataSync
oneLiner: Fast, managed bulk data transfer from on-prem/other clouds into AWS storage.
whatItIs: DataSync is AWS's managed online data-transfer service for moving large amounts of file and object data — from on-prem NFS/SMB shares, HDFS, or other clouds (including S3-compatible stores) into AWS storage like S3, EFS and FSx. It handles the hard parts of bulk transfer: parallelisation, encryption in transit, integrity verification, retries and incremental syncs, at speeds far beyond scripting your own copy. Where DMS moves databases, DataSync moves files and objects. It's a common way to seed a data lake with existing datasets or keep an on-prem file store synced to S3.

inPractice.narrative: A company has terabytes of files on an on-prem NAS that need to land in an S3 data lake. Rather than script fragile copies, they deploy a DataSync agent on-prem and run a task that transfers the data to S3 in parallel — encrypted, verified, and resumable — then schedule incremental syncs to keep new files flowing. Once in S3, Glue and Athena take over. DataSync is the ingestion on-ramp that gets bulk file data into AWS reliably.

coreConcepts.detail: For on-prem sources a lightweight DataSync agent runs near the data; a task defines source, destination and options. Cloud-to-cloud transfers may not need an agent.
Parallelised, encrypted, integrity-checked transfer with automatic retries — far more reliable and faster than hand-rolled rsync/scripts at scale.
After the first copy, DataSync transfers only changes, so it can keep a source and S3 continuously in sync on a schedule.
Writes to S3, EFS and FSx (and can move between them), making it a general ingestion tool for AWS file/object storage.
DataSync is for online (network) transfer; for datasets too big for the network in reasonable time, the AWS Snow family ships physical devices instead.
Throttling and scheduling let you control network impact and run large transfers during off-hours.

whenToUse: Bulk-loading on-prem files/objects into an S3 data lake.
Ongoing scheduled sync from on-prem NAS/HDFS to AWS.
Migrating file data between clouds or into EFS/FSx.
Reliable, verified transfer of large datasets over the network.
Seeding analytics storage with existing file archives.
whenNotToUse: Datasets too large to move over the network in time — use the Snow family (offline).
Small ad-hoc copies where the CLI/SDK is simpler.

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Managed online bulk file/object transfer into AWS.

keyFacts.label: Sources
keyFacts.value: On-prem NFS/SMB/HDFS, other clouds, S3-compatible stores.

keyFacts.label: Offline sibling
keyFacts.value: AWS Snow family for network-impractical volumes.

pricingShape: DataSync bills per gigabyte of data transferred, plus the usual underlying costs (destination storage, and egress on the source side if applicable). There's no standing instance charge — you pay for what you move, so a one-time seed is a one-time cost while a recurring sync costs per run by the changed data. Levers: use incremental syncs so you only pay to move new/changed files, schedule and throttle to fit bandwidth, and for truly massive first-loads compare against the Snow family's offline shipping economics.
gotchas: The on-prem agent needs deploying and network access — plan connectivity and bandwidth up front.
Per-GB pricing means a full re-copy is costly; rely on incremental syncs after the first load.
It moves files/objects, not databases — use DMS for database replication.
Network transfer of petabytes can be impractically slow/expensive — the Snow family may be cheaper/faster.
Large transfers can saturate links; use bandwidth throttling and off-hours scheduling.

equivalents.name: Storage Transfer Service
equivalents.note: Managed bulk transfer into Cloud Storage; GCP's analogue (Transfer Appliance for offline).

equivalents.name: Azure Data Box
equivalents.note: Bulk transfer into Azure; Data Box covers offline, AzCopy/Storage Mover the online path.
